FOR GROWN-UPS

Every sheet follows five friendly steps.

The sheets keep one shape on purpose: after the first sheet your child already knows how to play the next one. The same five moves, new good habits.

  1. 1

    Circle it

    One right picture to circle — looking closely is the whole game.

  2. 2

    Match them

    Draw lines from the left side to the right side.

  3. 3

    Choose one

    Two choices — tick or circle the one that fits.

  4. 4

    Trace it

    Big tracing words, any color you like.

  5. 5

    Draw it

    The last box is all yours — draw!

Nothing is scored and nothing is timed. A sheet your child saved is a sheet finished — the “Cleared!” ribbon is theirs to keep, saved separately for each child you set up in My Classroom.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Life skills are not learned from a poster — they are practised on real days, with real hands. These sheets give the practice a picture: your child circles the child washing hands, and somewhere that evening they will wash theirs with a little more purpose. Keep the words big, the praise specific and the sessions short. The drawing layer is a real pencil as far as a four-year-old is concerned, and saving their finished sheet — their own circles and squiggles over the real artwork — is the proudest ending there is.

Wash Your Hands — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns hand-washing from a reminder into a routine your child runs alone: when to wash, the four steps in order, and the song that makes the scrub last long enough to matter.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Hand-washing means scrubbing every part of both hands with soap and water — fronts, backs, between the fingers, the thumbs and up the wrists — then rinsing and drying.

What does it mean?

Soap does not just rinse dirt away; it loosens the invisible stuff so the water can carry it off. The scrubbing time matters far more than the water temperature or the color of the soap.

What does the child need to know?

The moments that need washing: before eating, after the toilet, after playing outside, after petting animals and after a nose-blow or a cough. The four steps in order — water on, soap, scrub, rinse — then a towel.

Why this matters

Hands are the main road germs take into bodies. A child who washes without being asked misses fewer days of preschool and carries fewer colds home to the whole family — the habit protects everyone at once.

What it teaches

Sequencing (four steps in order), self-care independence, cause-and-effect thinking — "I wash, we stay well" — plus the fine-motor work of rubbing every single finger.

Words to learn

soapscrubrinsegermsbubblesdry

Say this to your child

“"Soap makes bubbles, and bubbles do the work. We scrub the fronts, the backs, between the fingers and up the wrists while we sing our song — then rinse it all away and dry. That is how hands get properly clean."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name the skill: washing hands, one of the big-kid habits.
  2. Point out what the picture really shows — the boy at the basin, soap bubbles climbing up to his wrists, water still running from the tap.
  3. Move to the real sink and walk the four steps with your child leading and you narrating.
  4. Sing while scrubbing — about as long as singing happy birthday twice — so the scrub covers between the fingers, the thumbs and the wrists.
  5. Agree together on the washing moments in your family day, then let your child be the one who remembers them.

Look closer at the picture

Look at the picture together: where do the bubbles reach — only the palms, or higher up the wrists? What is the tap doing? What do you think the boy in the green shirt is singing? Is anyone watching him wash?

Ask your child

"When do we wash our hands?" "Which parts of your hands are the sneakiest — where does soap forget to go?" "What does the tap give us first, water or soap?" "What do we do after the rinse?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might chant the four steps — "water, soap, scrub, rinse!" — sing a made-up washing song at the sink, or proudly report "I scrubbed my thumbs, the sneaky ones!"

Out in the real world

Washing happens in many sinks: at home, at preschool, in restaurant bathrooms, at the petrol-station sink before a road-trip snack. Every sink is the same four steps — that is exactly the point to name out loud.

Try it together

Pepper experiment: sprinkle pepper on water in a bowl. Dip one finger in plain water — pepper clings to it. Dip a soapy finger — the pepper dashes away. That dash is what soap does to germs: visible, safe and unforgettable.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the four steps? When do we wash? Show me how you scrub between your fingers." Four steps in order plus wiggling fingers = lesson landed.

Parent tips

Keep a step stool living at the bathroom sink so "I can do it myself" is always true. Praise the remembering, not just the result — "you washed all by yourself" beats "look how clean" at this age.

Staying safe

Hot water can scald little hands — warm is plenty. After touching raw egg or meat at cooking time, everyone washes, and the grown-up does the final re-wash.

This lesson pairs with the Wash Your Hands flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Brush Your Teeth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes tooth-brushing a routine your child owns — with the honest division of labour that keeps four-year-old teeth healthy: they brush first, you finish the job.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Brushing means cleaning every tooth — the fronts, the backs and the chewing tops — with a soft brush and a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste, for about two minutes, twice a day.

What does it mean?

Food leaves a sticky film on teeth; the brush sweeps it off before it can make holes. Fluoride in the paste strengthens the enamel so the holes never start. The back teeth do the most chewing and get missed the most.

What does the child need to know?

Morning and night are the two brush moments, and the night one matters most — during sleep, saliva dries up and stops guarding the teeth. Spit, do not rinse: the fluoride keeps working after the brush is away.

Why this matters

Baby teeth hold the spaces for adult teeth and make chewing and clear speech possible. Cavities at four are painful and mostly preventable — two honest minutes a day is the whole trick.

What it teaches

Fine-motor control (small circles, reaching the back teeth), sequencing (brush, spit, rinse the brush), body awareness, and the responsibility pride of owning a real daily job.

Words to learn

toothbrushtoothpastefluoridespitenamelcavity

Say this to your child

“"Little circles on every tooth — the fronts, the backs, and the big chewers at the back that we almost never see. When you finish, I do the final polish. Then you spit the foam out — no rinsing, so the toothpaste keeps guarding your teeth all night."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name what the boy holds — the brush in one hand, the toothpaste in the other.
  2. Count teeth together in a mirror: the top row, the bottom row, the big ones hiding at the back.
  3. Demonstrate little circles on your own teeth, then hand over the brush and let your child copy.
  4. Make two minutes concrete: a sand timer, a brushing song or the brush’s own tune beats "keep going" every time.
  5. Finish with the parent pass — you take the brush and polish the back teeth while your child tips their head back and looks at the ceiling.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy holding in each hand? What color is his toothbrush? Where has the foam climbed — his teeth, his lip? What is he standing behind? Do we brush right there too?

Ask your child

"Why do we brush at night?" "Which teeth are the hiding ones?" "What do we do with the foam — rinse it or spit it?" "Who does the final polish in our family?"

What your child can say or do

"I brushed the back teeth!" "Spit, no rinse!" Your child may count every tooth out loud as they brush, or sing the brushing song to a doll before brushing their own.

Out in the real world

The routine travels: home bathroom, grandma’s house, holidays, hotel sinks. A travel brush in the overnight bag makes the rule portable — same two minutes, new sink, and your child sees the habit does not bend.

Try it together

Eggshell experiment: soak one eggshell piece in cola overnight and one in water — the cola shell stains and roughens. "That is sugar water on tooth shells." Then brush a hard-boiled egg with toothpaste and watch the cleaning happen.

Understanding check

Ask: "How long do we brush? What do we do with the foam? Who polishes the back teeth?" Two minutes, spit, grown-up pass = landed.

Parent tips

Let your child choose the brush color and the paste flavor — ownership halves the battle. Swap brushes every three months and after any illness. If brushing meets resistance tonight, let them brush YOUR teeth first; the giggle opens the door.

Staying safe

Toothpaste is for brushing, not eating — a smear the size of a grain of rice is plenty at four, and brushing happens with a grown-up nearby. Falling asleep with a bottle of milk or juice is the fastest road to cavities there is.

This lesson pairs with the Brush Your Teeth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Use the Toilet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson walks the complete toilet routine in order and hands your child the words — and the pride — of running it alone, including what happens when the body’s timing misses.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Using the toilet alone means hearing the body’s signal in time, going, wiping properly, flushing and washing hands — the whole chain, every time.

What does it mean?

The body whispers before it shouts; noticing the whisper early is the real skill. Wiping front to back keeps germs away from the body. Flushing and washing close the loop so the routine is truly finished.

What does the child need to know?

The full sequence: signal, trousers down, sit, do it, wipe front to back, trousers up, flush, wash. The signal can arrive mid-game — pausing play to go is the hard and important part at four.

Why this matters

Toilet independence is a doorway skill: it is what preschool expects, what sleepovers need and what your child’s own dignity wants. A child who runs the whole routine never has to interrupt play to find help.

What it teaches

Interoception (reading body signals), sequencing a six-step routine, hygiene habits, the gross-motor work of clothes on and off, and the self-respect of a job done fully alone.

Words to learn

toiletflushwipewashroutineaccident

Say this to your child

“"Your body whispers before it shouts. When you feel the whisper, you go — trousers down, sit, do it, wipe front to back, up, flush, and the last step you already know: soap. If your body ever surprises you, that is okay. Accidents are just practice that arrived early."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name the proud face — this is a picture of someone who did the whole job himself.
  2. Walk the sequence aloud on a calm day: trousers, sit, wipe front to back, up, flush, wash.
  3. Agree on the signal words your child will use to say they need to go — then honour them instantly, every single time.
  4. Practise the clothing part on its own: underwear and trousers up and down is a real skill at four.
  5. Make the plan for misses before they happen: "accidents happen, we change calmly, nobody is in trouble."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: where is the boy sitting? What color is the toilet seat? Where are his trousers — up or down? Is his face worried or happy? What will he do when he is finished?

Ask your child

"What does your body tell you when it is time?" "Which way do we wipe?" "What comes after the flush?" "What do we do if there is an accident?"

What your child can say or do

"I need to go — the whisper!" "I did it all by myself." Your child may retell the whole sequence in order like a story, or proudly report that a friend had an accident at preschool and "it was okay".

Out in the real world

Every toilet becomes familiar with the same routine: home, preschool, restaurants, aeroplanes, friends’ houses. The steps never change — that predictability is what makes new places easy instead of scary.

Try it together

Routine cards: draw or print the six steps, shuffle them, and let your child lay them in order on the bathroom door. Then a plush toy "needs to go" and your child coaches it through every step, wipes and all.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are all the steps? Which way do we wipe? What happens after an accident?" Full sequence, front to back, calm answer = landed.

Parent tips

Never rush or hover at the door — pressure creates the accidents it fears. Keep spare clothes at preschool and in the car so a miss is a two-minute fix. Praise the pause — "you stopped playing to go, that is the hard part" — more than the result.

Staying safe

Wiping front to back is a health rule, not a preference. Bathroom floors get wet — no running in socks. Cleaning products and toilet brushes stay out of reach; washing hands is your child’s job, scrubbing the toilet is not.

This lesson pairs with the Use the Toilet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Blow Your Nose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches nose-blowing the way it is actually learned: first the feeling of air moving out, then one nostril at a time, gently — with the bin-and-wash finish built in from day one.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Blowing your nose means pressing one nostril closed and pushing air gently out of the other into a tissue — clearing the nose instead of sniffing everything back.

What does it mean?

A blocked nose is mucus that needs a way out; blowing gives it one. Blowing HARD pushes mucus toward the ears and can make them ache — gentle and often beats strong and rare.

What does the child need to know?

The full routine: fetch a tissue, blow one nostril gently, then the other, fold the tissue closed, bin it, wash hands. Tissues live at child height so the whole chain is always reachable.

Why this matters

A child who can clear their own nose hears better, eats better, sleeps better and spreads fewer colds. It is also a skill preschool quietly expects — and the difference shows at circle time.

What it teaches

Breath control (air out on purpose), body awareness, hygiene habits, fine motor (pinching one nostril, folding the tissue) and self-care confidence that carries into every sniffly day after.

Words to learn

tissuenostrilblowgentlebinsniff

Say this to your child

“"Press one side closed and blow gently out the other — like sighing through your nose, not shouting. Soft wins here: blowing hard pushes everything toward your ears and makes them ache. Then the tissue goes in the bin and your hands get soap."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the boy holding, and with how many hands? Then demonstrate on yourself, mirror to mirror, so your child can see a nostril up close.
  2. Teach the feeling before the skill: hold a tissue in front of your child’s mouth and have them blow air OUT — feeling air move is the click that makes nose-blowing make sense.
  3. Practise one nostril at a time: press the left side closed, gentle blow on the right, then swap.
  4. Make the finish part of the skill: fold the tissue, drop it in the bin, wash hands — every time.
  5. Put tissues at child height in every room where noses happen, so the whole chain is always within reach.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy holding against his nose? How many hands is he using? Where are his eyes looking? Does his face look cross or calm? What happens to the tissue after?

Ask your child

"How many nostrils do we blow at a time?" "What happens if we blow too hard?" "Where does the tissue go afterwards?" "What do we wash after blowing?"

What your child can say or do

"One nostril, gentle blow!" Your child may run the steam game on a teddy, or call from the bathroom: "I binned it all by myself!"

Out in the real world

Cold season is the practice season: the tissue box in the car, the packet in your bag, the preschool hook where their own box hangs. Every sniffly day is the lesson — gentle blow, bin, wash.

Try it together

Feather races: blow feathers across the table with a straw to strengthen out-breath control. Replay the steam game on the first real sniffly day — air moving OUT is the whole skill.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many nostrils at a time? Hard or gentle? What are the three finish moves?" One, gentle, fold-bin-wash = landed.

Parent tips

Cheer the attempt, not the result — early nose-blowing is mostly air noise. Never redo the wipe silently; hand a fresh tissue and let them try again. A child who masters this before the next cold is a different child entirely.

Staying safe

Snot carries colds — the bin-and-wash finish is what keeps the family well, so treat it as firmly as the blow itself. Tissues are the tool for noses, not sleeves or fingers, and clean hands are always the finish.

This lesson pairs with the Blow Your Nose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Clean Up After Eating — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson ends the meal properly: your child learns that eating is not finished when the belly is full — it is finished when the spot is clear — and that the clear-away is their own three-move job.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Cleaning up after eating means carrying your own plate and cup to where they go, sweeping crumbs into the bin, and pushing the chair back in — the meal’s final chapter.

What does it mean?

In restaurants and preschool canteens, trays go to a rack because meals have an end-to-end shape: eat, clear, done. Learning that shape at home makes every eating place outside it feel familiar instead of confusing.

What does the child need to know?

The three moves: plate and cup to their place, crumbs to the bin, chair pushed in. Where "their place" is depends on the house — deciding YOUR places together is part of the lesson.

Why this matters

Clearing one’s own spot is the first chore that is entirely self-contained — no help needed, no technique required, a finish line visible from the first bite. That is why it sticks: the win is always winnable.

What it teaches

Task completion (seeing a job through to its true end), sequencing, ownership and contribution — "I am someone who helps this family run" — plus careful carrying, an underrated motor skill.

Words to learn

platecupcrumbsbinclearfinished

Say this to your child

“"Belly full? Then the job starts. Plate and cup go to their place, crumbs go in the bin, chair goes back in. Three moves and the meal is truly finished — and everyone in this house clears their own spot, even grown-ups."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the boy carrying? Where is he putting it? Name the skill — the meal is not over until the spot is clear.
  2. Walk YOUR kitchen or table: agree where the plate goes, where the cup goes, where crumbs go. The card names the job; your home names the places.
  3. Start the routine tonight with the three moves done side by side, then step back one move at a time.
  4. Add the chair push-in as the ceremonial finish — the small click that says "this meal is complete".
  5. Let the routine be the boss, not you: "what comes after the last bite?" becomes your whole prompt.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy carrying? What is sitting on top of the plate? Where is he putting them — the shelf with the stacked plates, or the bins below? What color is his cup?

Ask your child

"What are the three moves?" "Where does your plate live in our kitchen?" "What do we do with crumbs?" "What is the very last move before the meal is done?"

What your child can say or do

"Belly full, plate away!" Your child may quiz YOU at dinner — "Daddy, where does your cup go?" — or narrate the three moves like a game show host.

Out in the real world

The skill travels to every eating place: the tray rack at the food court, the plate scrape at grandma’s, the preschool lunch table. Each one is the same three moves with new locations — name them as you go.

Try it together

Restaurant at home: set a tray, "serve" the meal, then play the return-to-the-rack moment with your child as both waiter and customer. Swap roles — being the waiter who clears is the practice; being the customer who clears is the proof.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three moves? Where does your plate go? What tells us the meal is really finished?" Three moves, right place, chair pushed in = landed.

Parent tips

Start small — carry the plate only, you handle scraping and washing. The habit outranks the technique; technique comes with height and years. Never redo their clear-away in front of them; if the cup must move later, move it quietly.

Staying safe

Plates and cups break when dropped — carry one thing at a time, two hands, walking feet. Sharp cutlery and hot pans stay grown-up jobs; your child’s cargo is the safe, unbreakable set.

This lesson pairs with the Clean Up After Eating flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Eat Healthy Food — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes healthy eating out of lecture territory and into the child’s hands: what "strong food" is, why plates look like rainbows, and how a shopper’s choice at the shop becomes a braver fork at dinner.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Eating healthy food means filling your plate with things that grow — vegetables, fruits, grains, proteins — the "every day" foods that build bodies, alongside small "sometimes" treats.

What does it mean?

Different foods do different jobs: some build muscles, some give quick energy, some help eyes and skin. A plate with many colors usually means many jobs getting done at once.

What does the child need to know?

The division of jobs: grown-ups choose and serve the food; children decide what and how much to eat from what is offered. New foods may need to appear ten times before the first bite — that is normal, not stubborn.

Why this matters

Eating habits form in the preschool years and last. A child who helps choose, wash and name vegetables eats braver — and a family with the every-day/sometimes language stops arguing about treats, because the rule is the rule, not the mood.

What it teaches

Vocabulary for food and colors, sensory bravery (look, smell, touch, lick, taste — in that order), decision-making within limits, and the body-awareness of noticing which foods make play feel strong.

Words to learn

vegetablesfruitrainbowtastestrongsometimes-food

Say this to your child

“"Rainbow food makes bodies strong. Your job is to taste; my job is to serve. You never have to love it — you just have to say hello to it. Say hello with your eyes, your nose, your fork — and one day, your mouth."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: name every food you can actually see on the boy’s plate — the green broccoli trees, the orange carrots, the purple grapes, the red strawberries, the apple slices.
  2. Ask which of those your child ate this week, and which is the "never tried one" — every plate has one.
  3. At the next shop, let your child choose ONE new fruit or vegetable; children eat braver when they chose the food themselves.
  4. Put the chosen food on the plate without pressure — serving it is the win, eating it is theirs.
  5. Keep the every-day/sometimes language alive at every meal: "broccoli is an every-day food; cake is a sometimes food."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy eating from his fork? How many foods can you count on his plate? Which ones are green? Which one is purple? Has he taken a bite already — how can you tell?

Ask your child

"Which foods on this plate have you tried?" "What does a new food smell like before it gets a taste?" "What is an every-day food? What is a sometimes food?" "Which food would you pick at the shop?"

What your child can say or do

"I tried one bite!" "That’s a sometimes food." Your child may rank plate colors — "two greens today!" — or report that their new vegetable said hello back.

Out in the real world

The shop is the classroom: the vegetable aisle is a color hunt, the fruit scale is a weighing game. Cooking adds more — washing tomatoes, tearing lettuce, stirring batter — hands in the food make mouths braver about the same food.

Try it together

Rainbow dinner chart: a paper plate with six color wedges; each meal, your child stickers the wedge for every color eaten. The game ends when nobody needs it — the rainbow has become the habit.

Understanding check

Ask: "Whose job is serving and whose is tasting? How many times might a new food say hello before we taste it? Name one every-day food and one sometimes food." Parent serves, ten hellos, two right answers = landed.

Parent tips

Never bribe with dessert — it teaches that vegetables are the bad part. Keep portions child-sized; a mountain of new food guarantees a no. Model eating the food yourself with visible enjoyment; children copy appetites before they copy advice.

Staying safe

Grown-ups cut grapes, cherry tomatoes, nuts and other round, hard foods into small pieces — whole ones are a choking risk at four. Wash fruit and vegetables before eating, and keep raw dough and unpasteurised drinks off the menu.

This lesson pairs with the Eat Healthy Food flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Get Dressed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson breaks dressing into its real steps and gives the mornings back to your child: the order that works, the night-before trick, and the calm voice for the shirt that gets stuck.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Getting dressed alone means putting clothes on in a sensible order — underwear, then shirt, then trousers, then socks and shoes — fastening what can be fastened and asking for help only for the tricky bits.

What does it mean?

Clothes have a logic: what sits closest to the body goes on first; tags go at the back; the head hole is stretchy and the sleeves are tunnels for arms. Once the logic clicks, every new garment is the same puzzle in new cloth.

What does the child need to know?

The two supporting skills: choosing (decided the night before, not mid-morning rush) and ordering (top before trousers or trousers before top — either is fine, but it must be a plan). The shirt-over-head moment is the one that traps four-year-olds; the trick is arms first, then head.

Why this matters

Dressing independently is the morning’s first win, and its shadow stretches across the day: a child who dressed themselves arrives at breakfast already capable. It also quietly builds the fine-motor strength that buttons, zips and later pencils demand.

What it teaches

Fine-motor control (pushing arms through, pulling waistbands), sequencing a multi-step routine, spatial thinking (front, back, inside-out) and frustration tolerance — the shirt WILL get stuck, and that is the lesson working.

Words to learn

shirtsleevestagstretchyorderzip

Say this to your child

“"Every piece has a home: underwear first, then the shirt, arms make the tunnels, head walks through, trousers up, socks last. When something sticks, you say ‘help please’ — and when it goes in backwards or inside-out, we just flip it. Clothes always forgive."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy is pulling a yellow shirt over his head with one arm already through — name exactly that moment, because it is the hard one.
  2. Walk the order with your child’s own clothes: underwear, shirt, trousers, socks. Say the order out loud as a chant.
  3. Teach the stuck-shirt fix: arms through first, then pull the head hole over — "arms make the tunnel, head walks through."
  4. Lay out tomorrow’s clothes together at bedtime, in the order they go on, so the morning has no decisions left in it.
  5. Narrate like a sports commentator while your child dresses — no hands-on help unless the ask comes first.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what color is the boy’s shirt? How many arms can you see — has one gone through yet? Where is his head — in the shirt or still out? What is he wearing on his feet so far?

Ask your child

"Which goes first, the shirt or the socks?" "What do we do when the head gets stuck?" "What could the tag tell us about the front and the back?" "What did we lay out last night?"

What your child can say or do

"Arms make the tunnel!" "I did it — look, look!" Your child may dress a doll in the same order, chanting the steps, or announce the day’s clothing plan at breakfast.

Out in the real world

Dressing happens in many places: bedrooms, swimming-lesson changing rooms, grandma’s house after a sleepover, the beach towel change. The same order works everywhere — and elastic waists travel better than buttons.

Try it together

Dress-the-ted relay: a bear, a child-sized shirt and a timer that nobody checks. Your child dresses the bear, then themselves, then "judges" which outfit has fewer twists. Slow is fine — accuracy is the game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes on first? What is the stuck-shirt fix? What did we lay out last night?" Underwear first, arms-then-head, correct clothes = landed.

Parent tips

Choose clothes that forgive: elastic waists, loose necks, velcro shoes. Buttons and zips arrive on their own schedule; struggle is the practice, not a sign it is too hard. Buy the next size with tomorrow in mind — tight sleeves turn winners back into babies.

Staying safe

Drawstrings on hoods and waists get cut off — they catch on slides and playground equipment. Dress for the weather you will meet, not the weather you see from the window, and never let a child stand while wriggling into trousers — sitting prevents the toppling.

This lesson pairs with the Get Dressed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Put On Your Shoes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the doorstep battle into a skill your child owns: how shoes tell you which foot they belong to, the sticker trick, and the timing rule that keeps the practice alive.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Putting on shoes means opening the shoe’s tongue, sliding the toes in, pressing the heel down and closing the strap — the right shoe on the right foot, every time.

What does it mean?

Shoes carry clues: the tongues lean toward each other like a closed book, the soles curve inward to match the feet. Velcro straps close with a satisfying rip; laces need fingers that are still under construction.

What does the child need to know?

The check: toes reach the front, heel sits down, strap closes flat. The sticker trick — one sticker cut in half, half in each shoe — turns "which foot?" into a matching puzzle: when the halves meet, the shoes are right.

Why this matters

Shoes are the gateway to outside. A child who needs an adult for shoes waits for the adult; a child who does shoes alone just — goes. The self-launch matters more than the neatness of the strap.

What it teaches

Fine-motor strength (opening the tongue, pressing heels), left-right body awareness, matching and puzzle logic, and perseverance — shoes resist, and the third attempt that succeeds is where the real learning lives.

Words to learn

shoestongueheelvelcrorightleft

Say this to your child

“"Tongue open wide, toes march in, heel sits down, strap goes RIP. When the sticker halves kiss each other, your shoes are on the right feet — check them yourself. If one fights back, take a breath and try again; shoes always give in third try."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy is sitting on the floor, working a blue sneaker onto his foot with both hands — name how he is sitting DOWN to do it, because sitting makes shoes easy.
  2. Play "which foot?" with both shoes: the tongues lean together when the shoes sit right.
  3. Teach the sequence out loud: tongue open, toes in, heel down, strap closed. Then let your child do it — slowly is allowed.
  4. Add the sticker halves if left-and-right keeps confusing: matching picture beats verbal rule at four.
  5. Guard the clock, not the task: leave five extra minutes so the practice can happen without anybody rushing.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: is the boy sitting or standing? How many shoes are on already? What color are his socks? What are his hands doing right now — can your hands copy them?

Ask your child

"How do the tongues tell us which foot?" "What do we do when a shoe fights back?" "Who checks the sticker halves?" "What comes after the heel sits down?"

What your child can say or do

"Tongue, toes, heel, RIP!" "They match — look!" Your child may hold both shoes up for a sticker check every single time, or teach the sequence to a teddy with impressive strictness.

Out in the real world

Shoe moments happen everywhere: the shoe rack at home, the swimming-pool bench, the soft-play shoe cubbies, the doorstep before the school run. Same tongue, same toes, same heel — a portable skill that starts the outing.

Try it together

Shoe-shop dramatics: line up every family member’s shoes and let your child "fit" them — matching pairs, finding the owner, closing the straps. Sorting, matching and strap practice all hide inside the game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the four moves? How do the stickers help? What do we do when a shoe fights?" Tongue-toes-heel-strap, matching halves, try again = landed.

Parent tips

Velcro first, laces much later — resist doing it for them when late; build in the five minutes instead. Praise the re-try louder than the success: "you tried again and WON" is the sentence that survives bad mornings.

Staying safe

Shoes protect feet outdoors — barefoot belongs on grass and indoor mats only. Check the fit every season: pressed toes mean pressed growth. Loose laces and flapping straps get fixed before running, or they become the trip they look like.

This lesson pairs with the Put On Your Shoes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pack Your Bag — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands the school bag to its true owner: your child learns to pack it the evening before, check it against a picture list, and treat a forgotten item as information — not a disaster.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Packing your bag means putting tomorrow’s things in tonight — book, bottle, hat, whatever the day needs — and checking the bag against a list before zipping it shut.

What does it mean?

Packing ahead beats packing in the morning because mornings have no slack: one missing shoe and the whole system stalls. The evening has time, calm and the chance to discover the missing thing while it can still be found.

What does the child need to know?

The real skill is not putting things IN — it is checking. A picture checklist (drawings, not words) by the bag lets a non-reader tick each item as it lands. Zip closed only after every picture has its tick.

Why this matters

Owning the bag plants the ownership of the whole school day. It also builds the memory muscle school will lean on for years — and it costs nothing: forgotten items at four are free lessons, forgotten at fifteen they are detentions.

What it teaches

Planning ahead (tomorrow-thinking is new at four), list-checking as a working-memory scaffold, responsibility for belongings, and honest recovery — "it was missing, we found a fix" — when something slips.

Words to learn

backpackpackcheckchecklisttomorrowzip

Say this to your child

“"We pack at night, when the house is calm. Book, bottle, hat — each one in, each picture ticked. Then we check with our eyes before we zip. If something is missing tomorrow, that is not trouble — that is information. We fix the list and try again."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the girl is sliding a red book into her blue backpack — name what she is doing NOW, which is tonight’s job, not tomorrow morning’s.
  2. Make the picture checklist together: draw the book, the bottle, the hat — one drawing per item, stuck by the bag.
  3. Pack tonight, not tomorrow: name each item, your child fetches it, ticks the picture, zips it in.
  4. Teach the check as a separate move: bag open, pictures in hand, one look each — then zip.
  5. When something is forgotten (it will be), debrief kindly at pickup: "what did the checklist miss?" and fix the list, not the child.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the girl putting into the backpack? What color is the book? What is she kneeling on — can you see her shoes? Is the bag open or closed? What would YOU pack for tomorrow?

Ask your child

"When do we pack — tonight or tomorrow morning?" "What is on your checklist?" "What do we do before the zip closes?" "What happens if something is missing?"

What your child can say or do

"Book — tick! Bottle — tick!" "I checked it all by myself." Your child may pack a teddy’s "school bag" with the same ceremony, or announce at dinner that packing happens after bath.

Out in the real world

Packing travels: the swimming bag on swim day, the library book bag, the picnic backpack, the hospital-visit bag when someone is poorly. Each is the same skill with a different list — let your child own the checklist design.

Try it together

Memory bag: put five household items in a backpack, let your child look for ten seconds, zip it, then name what is inside from memory. Unzip and check together — the check is the applause moment.

Understanding check

Ask: "When do we pack? What do we check before zipping? What do we say when something is missing?" Tonight, pictures-ticked, "information not trouble" = landed.

Parent tips

Resist packing it yourself in the morning rush — that steals the skill. Forgetfulness is the teacher, not the enemy: the day the book is missing, talk kindly and repack. Keep the checklist current — an out-of-date list teaches checking to be useless.

Staying safe

Bags stay light — a packed school bag should never weigh more than the child can lift with one hand. Straps go on both shoulders, and nothing sharp, hot or liquid-leaking rides in the same pocket as books.

This lesson pairs with the Pack Your Bag flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Put Clothes Away — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives clean clothes a finishing routine: your child stacks the folded pile, carries it, and puts every garment where it lives — with a drawer system that makes the whole job winnable.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Putting clothes away means taking the stack of clean clothes to where they live — the drawer, the shelf, the box — and placing each one where it belongs, ready to be found again.

What does it mean?

Clothes have homes like toys do. A garment that lands in its home is findable; a garment dumped anywhere is lost in practice. Two categories are enough at four — shirts here, trousers there — the rest is grown-up sorting.

What does the child need to know?

The moves: take the stack, walk it to the drawer, place the shirts, place the trousers, close the drawer. If the pile is big, two trips beat one wobbly tower. Lumpy folds are a win — they mean the child did it.

Why this matters

Children who know where their clothes live can dress without an adult — the dressing independence from earlier lessons depends on THIS lesson. Contribution at home is also quietly identity-forming: "I am someone this house needs."

What it teaches

Sorting into categories, spatial stacking (a tower that survives the walk), sequencing a multi-move job, ownership of a personal space, and the quiet pride of a drawer that opens to find exactly what was put there.

Words to learn

foldstackdrawershelfput awaytidy

Say this to your child

“"Clean clothes have homes, just like toys. You stack them like a sandwich, carry them with two hands — walking, not running — and each piece goes where it lives. The fold can be lumpy; the putting-away is the real work, and lumpy is proud work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy is stacking folded clothes — red on blue on yellow on green — into a big box. Name the colors and the order; stacking is half the job.
  2. Open the real drawer or basket your child will use. It must be reachable without asking — that is the design rule.
  3. Walk the job once together: stack, carry with two hands, shirts home, trousers home, close.
  4. Agree the two categories for your house: shirts and trousers is the classic start; anything else is yours.
  5. Hand the job over: from the next laundry day, the stack is theirs to deliver — you fold, they file.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy holding — how many folded clothes? Which colors can you see? Where are they going, the box or the floor? Is he kneeling or standing? What is he wearing on his feet?

Ask your child

"Where do your shirts live? And your trousers?" "How do we carry a tall stack?" "What do we do if the tower wobbles?" "Why does the drawer need to be low?"

What your child can say or do

"Shirt home, trousers home, all done!" Your child may invent a stacking order by color every laundry day, or forbid anyone else from touching "their" drawer — which is exactly the ownership working.

Out in the real world

Laundry day is the practice day: the pile comes off the line or out of the dryer, and your child files their own share. Hotels, holidays and grandma’s house all have drawers too — the homes just have different names.

Try it together

Laundry basket relay: two baskets at one end, empty drawer at the other. Your child stacks, carries, files, returns for the next load — against a song, not a clock. The stack that survives the walk wins the quiet cheer.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do clean clothes go? How many trips is a big pile? Whose drawer is it?" Their home, two trips, THEIRS = landed.

Parent tips

Do not refold in front of them — smooth the shirt later if you must, quietly. One low drawer or basket is all the infrastructure a four-year-old needs; ownership needs the right height, not more storage. Praise the delivery, not the folding.

Staying safe

Drawers and boxes stay closed when not in use — open drawers are climbing invitations and tripping hazards. Heavy items live in low drawers, never stacked above a child’s head, and the wardrobe door is a pinch-point to respect.

This lesson pairs with the Put Clothes Away flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sort the Laundry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns laundry day into thinking practice: your child learns the dark-and-light categories, holds up each piece to ask "which basket?", and discovers that chores can be matching games in disguise.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Sorting the laundry means putting clothes into groups before they are washed — dark colors in one basket, light colors in the other — and pairing the socks at the end.

What does it mean?

Colors bleed in warm water: a red shirt can turn a whole white load pink. Washing darks with darks and lights with lights keeps every garment the color it was bought as. It is a real reason, not an arbitrary rule.

What does the child need to know?

The method: hold up one piece at a time — "this basket or that one?" — and decide. Socks come off the line in pairs: two that match go together. The categories live in your house: colors and whites, or darks and lights.

Why this matters

Sorting by one attribute (color) is exactly the thinking skill behind maths grouping and science classification — it just happens to also be a job. Chores that feel like play get claimed by children instead of avoided.

What it teaches

Classification by attribute, one-at-a-time decision-making, visual matching (sock pairs), vocabulary of colors and categories, and the work ethic of a real task that really helps the family.

Words to learn

laundrybasketsortdarkslightspair

Say this to your child

“"We sort before we wash: colors with colors, whites with whites — because colors sometimes share a little of their color in the water, and we want every shirt to stay the color it was. You hold each one up and ask: which basket is home for you?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the girl holds a pink shirt over the pink basket and a blue shirt over the blue basket — name the match she is making.
  2. Set up YOUR two baskets on laundry day and name the categories out loud: colors and whites, or darks and lights.
  3. Play the holding-up question: one piece at a time — "this basket or that one?" — and let your child answer and drop.
  4. Finish with the sock hunt: pull the socks out and find their pairs. Two that match, folded together, into the drawer pile.
  5. Close the loop: when the machine is running, say why — "the colors stay with their friends so nobody bleeds."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the girl holding in each hand — what colors? How many baskets can you see, and what colors are they? What color clothes are already in the pink basket? And in the blue one?

Ask your child

"Why do we wash darks and lights separately?" "How do we choose a basket for one shirt?" "What do we do with the socks?" "What would happen if a red shirt washed with the whites?"

What your child can say or do

"This basket or that one?" Your child may quiz the whole family with the holding-up question, or proudly pair every sock on the sofa — mispairs corrected with the gravity of a detective.

Out in the real world

Sorting travels: the holiday laundry bag, the swimming-towel basket, the donation box for outgrown clothes. Each sort is the same question — which group does this belong to? — with new stakes.

Try it together

Sock memory: five pairs of socks, mixed face-down on the floor — flip two at a time to find pairs. When the game ends, all socks are pre-paired for the real drawer. Laundry, advanced by play.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why do we sort before washing? What is the holding-up question? What do we do with socks?" Colors-bleed reason, one-at-a-time, pairs = landed.

Parent tips

Keep the categories honest — if the baskets get muddled, the pink shirts will explain the rule better than any lecture. Let the child deliver the final sock verdict. Two categories only; sub-sorting can wait years.

Staying safe

Laundry pods and detergents look like sweets and are poison — they live up high, handled by grown-ups only. The washing machine door is a grown-up’s to open and close, and baskets on the stairs are an edge to walk, not a slide to ride.

This lesson pairs with the Sort the Laundry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tidy Up Toys — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes clean-up time a game with rounds and a finish line: every toy has a home, the tidying goes in rounds — cars, then animals — and a song gives the mess its ending.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Tidying up means putting toys back where they live when play is done — car to the car home, teddy to the teddy home — so the floor is ready for tomorrow’s play.

What does it mean?

Tidying is matching: every toy has a home it belongs to, and the game is walking each one there. Four-year-olds tidy in circles, not lines — they wander, restart and discover — so rounds ("cars home, then animals home") give the wandering a shape.

What does the child need to know?

The method: pick ONE category per round, finish it, then the next. A tidy-up song sets the finish line. Doing it WITH your child matters more than ordering them to — your calm company is the engine at four.

Why this matters

A child who can restore their own play space plays more bravely — big messes are only fun when they know the way back. Tidying also trains the follow-through muscle: play is not over until the room says so.

What it teaches

Categorising (toys by type or home), sustained attention across rounds, sequencing, respect for belongings, and the emotional skill of ending something enjoyable — the hardest transition of the preschool day.

Words to learn

tidyhometoy boxroundfinishfloor

Say this to your child

“"The toys are tired and it is time to walk them home. Cars home first — zoom, straight to the box. Then the animals — hop, hop. When the song ends, the floor is clear and tomorrow’s play is ready. I will take the animals if you take the cars."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy is returning a red car to a yellow toy box where a teddy already sits — two toys, two homes, one job.
  2. Give every toy a named home in your child’s room: "the car home", "the bear home". Unnamed homes do not get used.
  3. Tidy in rounds: "cars home first" — only cars — then "animals home." Rounds turn a mountain into a staircase.
  4. Start a tidy-up song when the first round begins; the song is the timer nobody fights.
  5. Do it WITH them, not at them: you take the animals, they take the cars — company first, order second.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy putting away — what color is the car? Who is already inside the box? Is the box yellow or blue? Is his mouth smiling or cross? What toys live at YOUR house that need a home?

Ask your child

"Which round comes first at our house?" "Where does the teddy live? The cars?" "When does tidy-up time end — how do we know?" "What happens to toys left on the floor overnight?"

What your child can say or do

"Cars home! Animals next!" Your child may sing the tidy-up song solo with added verses, or comfort a toy while walking it home — "don’t worry, you’ll come out tomorrow."

Out in the real world

Tidying happens beyond the playroom: the blocks at the library, the plates at the picnic, the kit bag after swimming. Same move — every thing back to its home — everywhere, which is why it is worth practising at home.

Try it together

Home-hunt: hold up one toy and ask "where does this one live?" — your child races it home. Reverse it at playtime: "who lives here?" pointing at the empty box. The homes become as familiar as the toys.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the rounds? What tells us tidy-up is finished? Where does the car live?" Cars-then-animals, the song, the box = landed.

Parent tips

Never tidy a child’s room as punishment — it poisons the skill. Keep floor homes low and reachable; a tidy-up that needs an adult’s arms is not a child’s tidy-up. A photo of the shelf with every toy home is a cheat sheet even non-readers can use.

Staying safe

Toy boxes with heavy lids need slow-close hinges or no lid at all — fingers are faster than lids. Small parts stay away from baby siblings, and the floor path to the bed stays clear for sleepy night-time feet.

This lesson pairs with the Tidy Up Toys flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Water the Plants — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your child something alive to look after: how to pour slowly at the soil, how to tell a thirsty plant from a swimming one, and what a new leaf says about the job they are doing.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Watering plants means giving the plant a drink at the soil — slowly, with a small can, only when the soil is dry — not drowning it with love every afternoon.

What does it mean?

Roots drink from the soil, not the leaves, so the water goes where the roots are. Too much water is worse than too little: roots that sit in a swamp rot. Most kid-plants die of enthusiasm, not neglect.

What does the child need to know?

The check before pouring: poke a finger into the soil — damp means wait, dry means drink. The pour: low and slow at the soil, until a little runs out of the pot’s bottom hole, then stop. Same day each week builds the rhythm.

Why this matters

Caring for a living thing is responsibility with visible results: the leaf that unrolls a week later is proof your child’s care worked. Patience, observation and gentleness all grow alongside the plant.

What it teaches

Responsibility and routine (same plant, same day), observation skills (soil, leaves, new growth), cause and effect across days — a genuinely delayed payoff — plus the fine motor control of a slow, two-handed pour.

Words to learn

watering cansoilrootsleavesthirstygrow

Say this to your child

“"This plant is yours. You check the soil with your finger — if it is dry, the plant is thirsty; if it is damp, it is still drinking from last time. Pour slowly at the roots, not the leaves, and stop when the soil has had enough. Plants drink little and often, just like us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy tips a light-blue can so water drips onto the dark soil of an orange pot — name WHERE the water lands, at the roots, not on the leaves.
  2. Do the finger test together: poke the soil. Damp or dry? Let your child be the one who declares the verdict.
  3. Practise the pour on empty ground or over the sink first: low, slow, two hands, stop when a little escapes the pot’s bottom.
  4. Give your child ONE plant that is completely theirs — a hardy one that forgives enthusiasm — and one watering day a week.
  5. Watch for the payoff together: new leaf, new height, a flower. Photograph it; celebrate it like a first step.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy holding — is it big or small? Where is the water going — on the leaves or the soil? What color is the pot? How many leaves does the plant have? What will happen after the drink?

Ask your child

"How do we know a plant is thirsty?" "Where does the water go — leaves or soil?" "What happens if we give too much?" "What did the plant do this week?"

What your child can say or do

"The soil is dry — drink time!" "A NEW LEAF!" Your child may introduce the plant to visitors by name, or report the soil verdict with the confidence of a scientist.

Out in the real world

Plant care is everywhere: the windowsill pot, the balcony boxes, grandma’s garden tomatoes, the classroom bean. Each is the same finger test and the same slow pour — your child now speaks fluent plant.

Try it together

Bean in a jar: a bean against the jar wall, wet cotton, and a drawing diary — one picture every two days. The root that grows before the shoot teaches the biggest secret of plants: the important work happens first, underground.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we check for thirst? Where do we pour? What happens with too much water?" Finger test, at the soil, swamp roots = landed.

Parent tips

Overwatering ends more kid-plants than neglect — teach "damp, not swimming" early. Pick a hardy plant so the job stays winnable. If the plant dies, treat it as science: what did we learn, what will we try next — then plant again.

Staying safe

Some house and garden plants are not for eating — hands water, mouths never. Spilled water is a slip hazard: the pour happens where spills get wiped. Grown-ups handle plant food, scissors and repotting; the watering can is your child’s whole toolshed.

This lesson pairs with the Water the Plants flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Use an Inside Voice — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches volume as a choice, not a scolding: three voice levels your child can name and switch between, the rooms that ask for each, and the game that makes quiet modes fun instead of forced.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Using an inside voice means matching your loudness to the place — whisper-voice or talk-voice inside, big voice saved for outside and for emergencies.

What does it mean?

Sound travels and touches people: in a shop, a bus or a library, big voices land on everyone. It is not that loud is bad — it is that places have needs. Outside, big voice belongs; inside, soft voice keeps everyone comfortable.

What does the child need to know?

Three levels to name: whisper (libraries, shops, baby-sleeping hours), talk (home conversation), big (the park, the garden, calling across the yard). The dial between them is your hand turning an imaginary knob.

Why this matters

A child who can control volume keeps the places they love open to them — cafés, cinemas, waiting rooms. Voice control is also the first self-regulation skill outsiders notice, and it is practised entirely through play.

What it teaches

Auditory awareness (hearing their own loudness), self-regulation (turning the dial on purpose), social empathy (how my sound lands on others) and the vocabulary of situations — each room has its rules and its reasons.

Words to learn

whispervoiceloudquietinsideoutside

Say this to your child

“"We have three voices: whisper, talk and big. Inside places like shops and libraries, we travel on whisper or talk. The big voice is not banned — it lives outside, at the park, where it can stretch its legs. Show me your whisper. Now your big voice. Now back to whisper."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the girl has a finger at her lips and the boy is leaning in to hear her whisper — name both jobs: the whisperer AND the listener.
  2. Demonstrate all three voices yourself, dramatically: whisper, talk, big. Let your child label each.
  3. Play the voice dial: your hand turns an invisible knob, your child matches the level — whisper, talk, big, back down.
  4. Name the rooms in your real week that ask for each voice: the shop, the library, the baby’s nap hour, the park.
  5. Catch the transfers: "that was shop-voice at the shop — you read the room all by yourself."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the girl doing with her finger? Who is she talking to? Is the boy’s face calm or cross? Why do you think he is leaning closer? What do our ears do when a sound is too big?

Ask your child

"Which voice fits the library? The park? The baby’s nap?" "How does the dial work?" "Why do big voices bother people inside?" "What voice are you using right now?"

What your child can say or do

"Whisper mode!" Your child may announce their own voice level before entering a shop, turn the imaginary dial on YOU mid-shout, or invent a baby-sleeping whisper for the hallway.

Out in the real world

Voice levels are everywhere once named: the library story-time whisper, the restaurant talk, the cinema hush, the playground roar. Each place is a level your child can now predict — and predictability is what makes outings calm.

Try it together

Sound detective: in a quiet place, whisper a sentence and let your child repeat it back; across the garden, use big voice for a call-and-answer. The gap between the two modes IS the lesson, played.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three voices. Which fits the shop? Where does big voice live?" Three levels, whisper-or-talk, outside = landed.

Parent tips

Inside voice lands as a game, never as a shush — children move toward what you name positively ("shop voice now") and away from what you hiss ("quiet!"). Model the switch yourself: your visible dial-turn teaches more than any reminder.

Staying safe

There is one place a big voice is a tool inside: calling for help when something is wrong. Teach the difference plainly — big voice for real trouble and outside play, never for getting your own way.

This lesson pairs with the Use an Inside Voice flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Say Please and Thank You — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the two magic words as tools, not tricks: please opens requests gently, thank you closes them warmly — practised through a trading game until they arrive on their own.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Saying please and thank you means asking with a soft word — "please" — and answering kindness with another — "thank you" — so that both sides of every exchange feel good.

What does it mean?

Please tells the other person you are asking, not demanding; thank you tells them their kindness landed. Neither word changes what you get — it changes the relationship around the getting.

What does the child need to know?

The pairing: please goes BEFORE receiving, thank you comes AFTER. Both are practised best in real mini-exchanges — a toy handed over, a cup passed, a door held — not in lectures about manners.

Why this matters

Politeness is social grease that lasts a lifetime: people lean toward children (and adults) who ask kindly and receive warmly. The habit planted at four through play becomes character by ten.

What it teaches

Social scripts (the words that open exchanges), empathy (noticing the giver), turn-taking language, self-control (pausing to add the word), and the confidence of knowing the universal password to every kindness.

Words to learn

pleasethank youaskreceivekindmanners

Say this to your child

“"Please is how we ask, thank you is how we receive. Watch: ‘May I have the truck, please?’ — here it is! — ‘Thank you!’ Two little words, and both of us feel warm. Your turn: ask me for anything you like, with the magic word."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy holds the truck OUT, the girl’s hands are clasped with joy — name both halves: the offering and the receiving.
  2. Act out the trade with a real toy: your child asks with please, you hand it over, they answer with thank you. Repeat until it flows.
  3. Swap roles so your child is the giver too — hearing "thank you" is half the education.
  4. Play the fade game: prompt less each week ("what do we say?" becomes a smile, then nothing) so the words learn to travel alone.
  5. Catch them doing it for real and name it exactly: "you said thank you all by yourself — I heard it."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy holding out? What are the girl’s hands doing — grabbing, or clasping happily? What do her happy hands tell us? What do you think she is about to say?

Ask your child

"Which word comes before we get something? Which comes after?" "How does it feel when someone says thank you to YOU?" "What do we say when we want a turn?" "Can you ask me for something with the magic word?"

What your child can say or do

"Truck, please!" "Thank you!" Your child may run shop-at-home with please-and-thank-you as the only accepted currency, or catch a grown-up forgetting a thank-you with gleeful justice.

Out in the real world

The magic words work everywhere: asking a shopkeeper for help, receiving a birthday plate, thanking the bus driver on the way off. Each real use is a rep — and every one lands on a real person who visibly warms.

Try it together

Kindness shop: stack toys as "goods", take turns being customer and shopkeeper — every transaction must include both magic words or the shop cannot open. Manners as the engine of the game, not the moral of it.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word asks and which word receives? Show me a please-and-thank-you trade right now." Before-and-after placed, one live trade = landed.

Parent tips

Prompt with a question, not an accusation — "what do we say?" keeps the child’s dignity while their mouth catches up. Never shame in public; practise in play. Fade prompts slowly: the goal is a habit that appears without you, and it will.

Staying safe

Politeness has a limit that must be taught in the same breath: a child may always say a firm NO to a stranger’s request, an unwanted touch or an unsafe ask — please does not open every door, and safety outranks manners, always.

This lesson pairs with the Say Please and Thank You flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Say Excuse Me — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the most versatile phrase in the politeness kit: excuse me covers passing through, joining a conversation and post-sneeze grace — and this lesson names all three jobs for your child.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Saying excuse me means using one polite phrase for three moments: when passing through someone’s space, when you need a grown-up’s attention mid-conversation, and after a burp, cough or sneeze.

What does it mean?

Excuse me is a small announcement: "I am here, I see you, I mean no bump." It replaces pushing past, shouting over and pretending nothing happened — each with a gentler, clearer alternative.

What does the child need to know?

The interruption rule is the crown skill: put a hand on the grown-up’s arm, wait for the pause, then speak. The hand says "I am waiting"; the pause is your opening. Passing through and post-sneeze are the quick uses.

Why this matters

A child with one polite interruption tool stops shouting, tugging and butting in — the three behaviours that exhaust adults. The phrase buys attention respectfully and gets it faster than any grab.

What it teaches

Impulse control (waiting for the pause), social awareness (reading when a conversation is busy), body-space respect, and conversation mechanics — knowing that talk has turns, and turns can be requested.

Words to learn

excuse mepassinterruptwaitpausesneeze

Say this to your child

“"Excuse me has three jobs. Walking through someone’s way: excuse me. Needing my attention while I talk: hand on my arm, wait for the pause, then excuse me. After a sneeze: excuse me — then the tissue does its work. One phrase, three kindnesses."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy walks past the girl with one hand raised, mid-hello; the girl holds her book and smiles — two people sharing one path politely.
  2. Name the three jobs of excuse me: passing through, joining a conversation, after a cough or burp. Children love collecting the uses.
  3. Teach the interruption rule with your own arm: their hand on your arm, your nod when the pause arrives, then they speak.
  4. Practise the doorway: walk through a real door together — who goes first, who says what, and the small body turn that keeps shoulders from bumping.
  5. Rehearse the sneeze line until it is automatic: "excuse me" — tissue — hands washed.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy doing — walking past or standing still? What is raised — his hand or his voice? What is the girl holding? Do they look squished or comfortable? Where are their feet going?

Ask your child

"What are the three jobs of excuse me?" "What does your hand do while it waits?" "What do we say after a sneeze?" "How do we pass through a doorway where someone stands?"

What your child can say or do

"Excuse me, passing through!" "Excuse me — can I say something?" Your child may apply the arm-hand rule with perfect ceremony, or catch the family cat’s rude doorway behaviour as a teaching moment.

Out in the real world

Excuse-me moments happen hourly: the supermarket aisle, the crowded bus, the doctor’s waiting room, the kitchen mid-conversation. Each is a live rep — passing, joining or post-sneeze — and your child now has the phrase ready.

Try it together

Busy-grown-up drill: you talk on a toy phone; your child practises the hand-arm-pause-speak chain until it is smooth. Swap roles so your child feels how pleasant a patient hand is compared to a shout.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three jobs. What does the waiting hand do? What follows a sneeze?" Three uses, waits-for-pause, excuse-me-and-tissue = landed.

Parent tips

Practise when nobody needs interrupting — calm rehearsals build the real skill. Answer the successful interrupt promptly: a child who waits politely and is then ignored learns that shouting works better. Keep the phrase warm, not robotic.

Staying safe

Excuse me is for space and turns — it is not permission to touch strangers or follow them. Bodies stay in their own space, hands ask before touching anyone, and an adult’s arm is for the waiting hand only when the adult is YOURS.

This lesson pairs with the Say Excuse Me flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Use Gentle Hands — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches gentle as a physical skill, not a personality verdict: the two-finger touch, the practice ladder from teddy to pets, and the positive naming that builds body control instead of shame.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Using gentle hands means touching softly and slowly — a light, careful touch for teddy bears, pets, babies and friends — watching how the touch lands and easing off when needed.

What does it mean?

Gentle is body control: the same hands that pat hard can stroke soft, and the difference is attention, not character. Four-year-old bodies are still building the brake system — gentle is the brake, practised daily.

What does the child need to know?

The practice ladder: teddy first (no feelings to hurt), then the real pet or baby with a grown-up beside. The two-finger touch is the classic starter — two fingers physically cannot whack. Watch the receiver: if they lean away, soften.

Why this matters

Children move toward what you name: "show me gentle" gives a target; "stop hitting" only names the problem. A child known for gentle hands gets invited closer — to hold the puppy, meet the baby, join the game — and closeness is its own reward.

What it teaches

Body control and soft-touch calibration, reading others’ signals (leaning in or away), empathy, impulse braking, and the pride of being trusted with fragile things — trust is the whole curriculum here.

Words to learn

gentlesoftstroketwo fingerscarefulcalm

Say this to your child

“"Gentle hands are slow hands and soft hands. Two fingers, like a butterfly landing. Watch teddy’s face — he likes it. When we meet a real pet or a baby, we use the very same touch, and we watch how they feel about it. If they lean away, we soften."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: two children, one teddy — both pairs of hands rest ON the bear softly. Name what their hands are doing: holding, not squeezing.
  2. Teach the two-finger touch: two fingers on teddy’s ear — "this is the gentle touch." Practise on your arm, their arm, the bear.
  3. Build the ladder aloud: teddy first, then pet or baby, grown-up always beside for the real ones.
  4. Narrate the receiver: "look — the puppy leaned IN, that means the touch was perfect."
  5. When roughness happens, skip the scolding and offer the target: "show me your gentle hands." They know the way.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what are the children holding? How many hands are touching the teddy? Are their fingers squeezing or resting? What are their faces doing? Can YOUR hands copy their hands right now?

Ask your child

"What do gentle hands feel like — show me on my arm." "Why do we practise on teddy first?" "What does it mean when a pet leans away?" "Who did you touch gently today?"

What your child can say or do

"Two fingers — butterfly landing!" "The cat leaned in, I did gentle!" Your child may stroke your cheek with visible concentration, or correct a doll’s rough hands with the family rules.

Out in the real world

Gentle moments are daily: stroking the neighbour’s dog with permission, holding the newborn cousin’s hand, touching library books, patting the class goldfish bowl-side. Each is a live rep with a receiver who gives feedback.

Try it together

Gentle-or-rough guessing game: you touch teddy two ways — a squeeze and a butterfly stroke — and your child names which is which, then performs both on demand. Naming the rough makes the gentle a choice.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the two-finger touch? Who do we practise on first? What do we do when the pet leans away?" Butterfly, teddy-first, soften = landed.

Parent tips

Offer the positive target, never just the prohibition — "show me gentle" beats "stop that" every time. Praise the touch you see, in the moment. If roughness keeps returning, add heavy-work play (squashing dough, wall pushes) — brakes need somewhere legal to work.

Staying safe

Real pets and babies are always two-person jobs: your child’s hands plus your supervision. Never leave a child alone with a dog, however gentle the history — and ears, tails, eyes and faces are look-with-eyes zones, not touch-with-hands zones.

This lesson pairs with the Use Gentle Hands flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Be Kind — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes kindness small, visible and repeatable: what kind hands, kind words and a kind face actually DO at four, one tiny mission a day, and the bedtime hunt that makes kindness a habit.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Being kind means noticing what someone else needs or feels and doing a small something about it — a greeting, a helping hand, a compliment, a share, a gentle wait.

What does it mean?

Kindness at four is concrete, not philosophical: it has hands (helping, holding, sharing), words (greetings, compliments, comfort) and a face (smiles, attention). Abstract "be good" teaches nothing; "give Sam the first turn" teaches everything.

What does the child need to know?

The daily mission: one small, named kindness per day, chosen in the morning, reported at bedtime. The bedtime kindness hunt — "when were you kind today? When was someone kind to you?" — closes the loop and trains the noticing.

Why this matters

Kindness is the social skill that opens every group: the second child invited into games, the first one trusted. It is also the most copyable virtue — children repeat what gets named, and named kindness multiplies.

What it teaches

Empathy (reading what another person needs), social initiative (acting without prompting), emotional vocabulary, moral identity — "I am someone who is kind" — and the attention training of the bedtime hunt.

Words to learn

kindkind wordshelpsharesmilenotice

Say this to your child

“"Kindness has hands, words and a face. Hands help and share. Words greet and comfort. A face smiles and pays attention. Each morning we pick one small kindness for the day, and at bedtime we hunt for it: when were you kind today? When was someone kind to you?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: a boy kneels to hold hands with a girl who is sitting on the floor — name the kind move: he came down to her level to help her up.
  2. Collect kind examples in your child’s own world: who helped you today? What did it look like? Hands, words or face?
  3. Start the daily mission: each morning, pick one tiny kindness — "give Grandma a compliment", "help carry the spoon", "greet the new boy."
  4. At bedtime, run the hunt: one kindness your child gave, one they received. Naming is the growing.
  5. Praise the specific, not the vague: "you shared your crayons without being asked" lands; "good boy" evaporates.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy doing — standing tall or coming down low? Whose hands are they holding? What are both faces doing? Has the girl started to stand up? What might have happened next?

Ask your child

"What did your hands do kindly today?" "What kind words can we say at the door tomorrow?" "How did it feel when someone was kind to you?" "What kindness mission shall we pick for tomorrow?"

What your child can say or do

"I helped Ilya carry his cup!" "Maya was kind to me — she waited for me." Your child may propose missions unprompted, or report a friend’s kindness with the delight of a good-news reporter.

Out in the real world

Kindness lives in plain sight: greeting the bus driver, holding a door, noticing a sad friend, letting the smaller child go first. The hunt trains the eyes; once noticed, these moments appear everywhere, and your child starts collecting them.

Try it together

Kindness jar: a pom-pom in the jar for every noticed kindness — given or received. The jar is never cashed in for prizes; the fullness itself is the point, and the counting at the end of the week is a happiness lesson.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three kinds of kind? What is the bedtime hunt? What was today’s mission?" Hands-words-face, given-and-received, the mission = landed.

Parent tips

Praise the specific deed, never the vague label — named kindness repeats, praised identity can wilt. Never force an apology or a hug; forced kindness is not kindness. Model it hardest when tired — they are watching exactly then.

Staying safe

Kindness keeps one sharp edge: children must know that saying NO, keeping their body safe and telling a grown-up about bad behaviour are also kind — to themselves. Being kind never means accepting an unwanted touch or keeping a scary secret.

This lesson pairs with the Be Kind flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Share Your Toys — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches sharing as the child’s own generous act — the held-out toy and its words — with the training wheels that make it real: timer turns, the special basket, and the words of offering.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Sharing your toys means offering something of yours to someone else — holding it out, saying the words — so two children get more fun than one toy alone can give.

What does it mean?

Sharing is generosity in motion, and it must be chosen to count. Forced sharing teaches resentment, not kindness. Real sharing has a vocabulary: "do you want a turn?", "here, you can go first", "let’s trade."

What does the child need to know?
