The tools that make sharing survivable at four: a timer for the wanted toys ("two minutes, then swap"), trades ("truck for crayons?"), and the special basket — toys that NEVER get shared when friends visit, decided before the doorbell rings.

Why this matters

A child whose ownership is respected shares more freely, not less — the special basket is the secret. Sharing is also the entry ticket to cooperative play, the developmental leap that makes real friendships possible at this age.

What it teaches

Generosity and its warm aftermath, negotiation (trades, timers, first-turns), empathy (reading the other child’s want), and ownership security — knowing what is mine so giving can be a gift, not a loss.

Words to learn

shareofferoffer wordstradeturnspecial basket

Say this to your child

“"This is yours, so the offer is yours to make. You can hold it out and say ‘do you want a turn?’ — or trade it, or take turns on the timer. Your special-basket toys never have to be shared; everything else can make two people happy at once. Look at their face when you offer — that smile is what giving does."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy holds the dump truck OUT — arms extended, not clutching — and the girl reaches with open hands. Name both: the offer and the welcome.
  2. Practise the words of offering with a real toy: "do you want a turn?" — the sentence is half the skill.
  3. Build the special basket before the next playdate: your child picks the never-shared toys; everything else is fair game for offers.
  4. Introduce the timer for the battle-toys: two minutes each, the swap is the rule, the timer is the referee — not you.
  5. Notice every offer that happens on its own and name it exactly: "you offered her the truck — look at her face."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: whose truck is it — who is holding it out? What are the girl’s hands doing? Are his arms stretched out or tucked in? Who is smiling — one of them or both? What happens next, do you think?

Ask your child

"What are the words of offering?" "Which toys live in your special basket?" "What does the timer do with the battle-toys?" "How does your friend’s face change when you offer?"

What your child can say or do

"Do you want a turn?" "Trade you — truck for crayons!" Your child may pack the special basket with ceremony before every playdate, or report an offer made at preschool with visible pride.

Out in the real world

Offering lives everywhere: the snack bag at the park ("want one?"), the crayons at the restaurant, the swing queue. Each real offer is a rep — and the returned smile is the curriculum’s own certificate.

Try it together

Trade-post: your child runs a "shop" where everything is free but must be asked for with the offer words. You play the customer who always says thank you and always offers something back. Generosity, practised as commerce.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the words of offering? What is the special basket? What does the timer do?" Offer-words, never-shared toys, referee = landed.

Parent tips

Never force a share — it builds a hoarder, not a giver. Respect the special basket absolutely; security grows generosity. Praise the offer louder than the loan, and let the returned smile do the moralising for you.

Staying safe

Sharing has a safety line: foods are never shared without a grown-up’s check — allergies live in other families’ snack boxes — and small toys that baby siblings could choke on stay out of the reach-and-offer zone.

This lesson pairs with the Share Your Toys flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Share and Take Turns — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the hardest wait of preschool into game mechanics: one toy, two players, turns named out loud and swapped on a count — until waiting becomes part of the fun instead of the end of it.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Taking turns means using one toy together in an agreed order — my turn, then your turn, then mine again — so both players get the whole fun, just at different times.

What does it mean?

A turn is a promise with a shape: it starts, it ends, then it returns. Unnamed turns feel like losing; named turns with visible swaps feel like a game with rounds. The words "my turn — your turn" ARE the mechanism.

What does the child need to know?

The starters: roll a ball back and forth, stack blocks alternately, push the truck on a count of ten. The wait-timer makes the wait concrete — a sand timer, ten counts, a short song — because "soon" means nothing at four.

Why this matters

Turn-taking is the training wheels of every friendship, game and conversation to come. A child who can wait for a named turn keeps the play going; a child who grabs ends it. The skill is worth more than any single toy.

What it teaches

Impulse control across a real delay, trust (my turn WILL come), turn vocabulary and sequence, joint attention (watching someone else play happily), and emotional recovery when a turn ends.

Words to learn

turnmy turnyour turnwaitswaptimer

Say this to your child

“"One truck, two players — so we take turns. My turn: vroom, vroom. Your turn — and I wait and watch, because my turn always comes back. We can count to ten for the swap, or let the sand timer run out. Waiting is part of the game — it is how two people get more fun than one."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: two children kneel facing each other, both hands on one truck — nobody grabbing, both smiling. Name the picture: one truck, two players, no fight.
  2. Play with one toy and two players: name the turns out loud — "MY turn... now YOUR turn" — with your hands showing the swap.
  3. Swap on a count of ten; let your child be the counter and the announcer — the announcer always knows the turn is coming.
  4. Add a visible timer for longer turns so the wait has a shape your child can watch drain.
  5. Graduate to real games with built-in turns: rolling a ball, alternate block-stacking — turn-taking IS the fun there.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: how many children are playing? How many trucks? Whose hands are ON the truck right now — one child or both? What are their faces doing? Are they kneeling face to face or back to back?

Ask your child

"Whose turn is it now? How will you know when it is yours?" "What can your hands do while you wait?" "What does the timer tell us?" "What happens after your turn ends?"

What your child can say or do

"My turn — your turn!" "Ten, nine, eight... SWAP!" Your child may announce turns for the whole family at dinner, or referee two toys’ turns with the gravity of a football match.

Out in the real world

Turns run the world: the slide queue, the swing wait, the video-game controller, the conversation itself. Each is a named turn your child can now spot — and the noticing turns resentment into anticipation.

Try it together

Turn-machine: a ball rolled back and forth with turns announced by the roller; blocks stacked alternately to build one tower together. Both games are turn-taking with the fun built in — the wait is the price of admission, paid gladly.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say when we swap? What does the timer do? Whose turn comes after yours?" Named turns, visible wait, yours-again = landed.

Parent tips

Practise turns on toys nobody cares about first; save the battle-truck for when the skill is warm. The waiting child needs a job — counting, announcing, timer-watching — idle waits curdle. Keep turns SHORT at four: many small turns beat one long hostage situation.

Staying safe

Turn-waiting ends where safety starts: a child never has to wait to call for help, and grabbing is corrected calmly, never with the toy snatched back — the grown-up’s hands model the turn-taking they are teaching.

This lesson pairs with the Share and Take Turns flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wait Your Turn — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives waiting a shape a four-year-old can hold: visible finish lines, the named wait — "three more turns" — and the calm stance that turns queue-time into watch-time instead of agony.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Waiting your turn means letting someone finish while you watch calmly, knowing your turn begins the moment theirs ends — on the slide, the swing, the queue, the speaking circle.

What does it mean?

Waiting hurts when it is endless and invisible; it works when it has a finish line you can see. The slide shows it best: she climbs, she sits, she slides, she steps off — now me. Patience at four is measured in visible minutes, not virtues.

What does the child need to know?

The tools: name the wait ("three more turns, then you"), stay near, narrate what you see ("she’s climbing up... she’s sitting... now it’s you!"), and celebrate the WAITING itself — "you waited for the whole slide" — not just the turn.

Why this matters

The slide queue is the first real queue of a child’s life, and queues run the world after it. A child who can wait a visible turn keeps their place in games, groups and conversations — and keeps friends, too.

What it teaches

Impulse control across a real delay, time concepts (first, next, then me), emotional regulation with a reward in sight, observation skills — and trust that the world keeps its promises about turns.

Words to learn

waitturnnextwatchpatiencequeue

Say this to your child

“"She is on the slide, so we watch and wait — and look how her turn ends: she steps off, and the slide is yours. I will name the wait: two more turns. Your hands can rest behind your back like the boy on the card. Waiting with a finish line is easy to hold."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the girl is sliding down the yellow slide, arms up; the boy stands beside it, hands behind his back, smiling. Name his hands — that stance IS the waiting skill.
  2. At the playground, narrate the finish line in real time: "she’s at the top... she’s sitting... she’s sliding... NOW it’s your turn."
  3. Give the wait a number when numbers apply: "two more turns." Vague waits stretch; numbered waits hold.
  4. Give the waiting hands a job: behind the back, or holding your hand, or watching the slider’s face — busy eyes make short waits.
  5. Celebrate the waiting out loud, immediately: "you waited for her WHOLE slide — that was patient!"

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: who is ON the slide? What is she doing with her arms? Where is the boy standing — on the ladder or beside it? What are HIS hands doing? Is his face angry or calm? Whose turn comes next?

Ask your child

"How will you know when your turn comes?" "What do your hands do while you wait?" "What can you watch while you wait?" "How long was your wait — one turn or two?"

What your child can say or do

"Two more turns — I’m counting!" "I waited the WHOLE slide!" Your child may adopt the hands-behind-back stance unprompted at the park, or narrate another child’s turn kindly from the queue.

Out in the real world

Queues are everywhere: the slide, the swings, the shop till, the bus door, the water fountain. Each is a wait with a visible finish line — and your child now has the tools to hold every one of them.

Try it together

Waiting race: line up three toys for one slide; your child is the queue-master who names whose turn is next and celebrates each waiter. Being the keeper of turns teaches the skill from the inside out.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes a wait easy to hold? What do your hands do? What do we say after a good wait?" Visible finish line, calm hands, "you waited!" = landed.

Parent tips

Stay near — waiting alone is a different, harder skill for later. Name the wait honestly; children forgive a known length, never a promised "soon" that never lands. If the wait collapses, step back to shorter waits and rebuild — patience is a muscle, not a mood.

Staying safe

Queues have edges: no climbing up the slide’s ramp to skip the wait, feet first only, and clear the bottom fast — the next slider is already coming. Grown-ups hold the queue rules; the child holds the wait.

This lesson pairs with the Wait Your Turn flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Listen Carefully — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson breaks listening into its three visible parts and builds the skill that school will run on: ears open, eyes on the speaker, body calm — then one two-step instruction at a time.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Listening carefully means pointing your whole self at the speaker — ears open, eyes looking, body still enough — and holding the words long enough to do what was asked.

What does it mean?

Listening is more than hearing: hearing is the sound arriving, listening is choosing to receive it. The three parts are visible on purpose — a child who cannot yet listen well can still DO ears-on, eyes-on, body-calm, and the mind follows the body.

What does the child need to know?

The practice unit is the two-step instruction: "get your cup, then sit at the table." Two steps is the four-year-old sweet spot; three is a stretch goal. The repeat-back comes BEFORE the doing: "say it to yourself first."

Why this matters

Whole-body listening is the master key of classroom life: instructions, stories, safety rules all arrive through it. A child who listens the first time keeps teachers warm and mornings smooth — the skill pays daily, forever.

What it teaches

Attention control, working memory (holding two steps), sequencing, self-regulation of the body, and communication respect — the listening half of every conversation your child will ever have.

Words to learn

listenearseyescalmstepsrepeat

Say this to your child

“"Listening is three things your body can do: ears open, eyes on me, body calm. Then the words get to land. I will give you a two-step mission — you say it back to yourself first, then do it. Cup first, then table. Say it. Now show me."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the grown-up kneels at the boy’s level with one finger raised, mid-sentence; he sits cross-legged, eyes on her, hands resting. Name all three listening parts on his body.
  2. Get to eye level and start with their NAME — a child listening across a room is half-listening. Name first, then talk.
  3. Play "what did I say": give one two-step instruction, have your child repeat it back, then do it. Repeat-back first, action second — every time.
  4. Stretch slowly: two steps mastered means try a three-step once a week — no more.
  5. Praise the listening, not just the doing: "you listened with your whole body" names the skill they can reuse.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: is the grown-up standing tall or kneeling low? What is her finger doing? Where is the boy sitting? Where are HIS eyes looking? Where are his hands? Can your body sit like that right now?

Ask your child

"What are the three parts of listening?" "What do we do with the mission before we do it?" "Why do I say your name first?" "What was today’s two-step mission?"

What your child can say or do

"Ears on, eyes on, body calm!" "Cup first, then table — done!" Your child may request missions at bedtime, or correct a teddy’s wandering eyes mid-story with the three-parts rule.

Out in the real world

Real listening gets tested daily: the preschool teacher’s morning instructions, the coach’s game rules, the safety words in the car park. Each is a two-step mission in the wild — and the repeat-back works everywhere.

Try it together

Simon-says-lite: you give two-step missions — "touch your nose, then hop once" — and swap roles so your child invents missions for you. Inventing instructions teaches what instructions feel like from the other side.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three parts. What comes first, the repeat-back or the doing? What is a two-step mission?" Three parts, repeat-back, one live mission = landed.

Parent tips

Deliver instructions at eye level with the name first — across-the-room shouting trains nobody. One mission at a time; instruction-piles bury the first step. If listening slips, check the basics: hungry, tired, mid-play — the skill needs a fed, calm brain.

Staying safe

Some listening is safety-critical: the word STOP from a trusted grown-up means freeze immediately, even mid-run — no questions first. Practise stop-and-freeze as a game so the real word has a rehearsed body behind it.

This lesson pairs with the Listen Carefully flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Follow Directions — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns instructions into missions: first/then language that gives a direction a shape, the say-it-back check that catches confusion early, and why one mission at a time is the rule that keeps success possible.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Following directions means hearing what is asked, saying it back to be sure, and doing it in order — first this, then that — until the mission is complete.

What does it mean?

Directions work when they are few, clear and ordered: "first shoes, then outside" beats a paragraph. The say-it-back step is not a test — it is a check that catches the mixed-up mission before the mixed-up doing.

What does the child need to know?

The first/then structure is the engine: "first we put on shoes, then we go out." Missions get followed; orders get ignored — the difference is framing. One or two directions at a time, at eye level, with a check: "what is the mission?"

Why this matters

The grown-up world runs on directions: classroom routines, safety steps, recipe steps, game rules. A child who can take a direction, check it and follow it through is equipped for every room they will ever enter.

What it teaches

Sequencing (first/then as flexible grammar), working memory, task completion, cooperation as a chosen role rather than submission, and the pride of the mission-accomplished report-back.

Words to learn

firstthenmissionordercheckdone

Say this to your child

“"This is a mission, not an order. First we hang the towel, then we find your water bottle. Say the mission back to me — good, you have it. Go! ... Mission accomplished? High five. One mission at a time, said back, done in order — that is how big people do things, and now so do you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the grown-up kneels with one finger up, mid-direction; the boy stands ready, listening with a happy face. Name the picture: a mission being delivered.
  2. Speak in first/then all day: "first socks, then shoes." "First dinner, then bath." The structure does the remembering for your child.
  3. Give one mission at a time, at eye level, then ask for the say-it-back: "what is the mission?" — before any feet move.
  4. Let your child collect the accomplishment out loud: "mission accomplished!" — the report-back is the ceremony that makes the skill lovable.
  5. When a direction fails, check the mission first: was it two missions pretending to be one? Split it.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the grown-up doing — how many fingers are up? Is she kneeling or standing? What is the boy wearing — what colors? What do you think the mission might be? Is he ready or already running?

Ask your child

"What comes first in our morning — socks or shoes?" "What do you say back before you start?" "What is the difference between a mission and an order?" "What was today’s mission?"

What your child can say or do

"First towel, then bottle — mission accomplished!" Your child may assign YOU missions at bedtime ("first pyjamas, then story"), or ask "what is the mission?" when a morning feels muddled.

Out in the real world

Directions run every outing: "first the trolley, then the shop", "first sunscreen, then the pool", the teacher’s line-up call, the coach’s warm-up. Each is a first/then your child can now catch in the air and run with.

Try it together

Mission-of-the-hour: write or draw one two-step mission on a card each day; your child draws it, says it back, completes it and stamps the card DONE. The card pile becomes a trophy shelf of followed directions.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the first/then shape? What do you say back before starting? How many missions at once?" First-then grammar, say-it-back, one = landed.

Parent tips

Frame as missions and the same words get followed — the framing is free. Check for understanding before compliance: confusion mimics defiance at four. Split any direction that fails into two smaller ones and watch the same child succeed.

Staying safe

Directions carry a rescue clause: if a child cannot do a mission safely — reach the shelf, cross the car park — the mission changes, not the child. And "stop" from a trusted grown-up outranks any mission in motion.

This lesson pairs with the Follow Directions flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ask for Help — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the sentence that keeps children safe and learning: "help, please" — when to try first, when to ask, WHO the trusted grown-ups are, and why asking is strength, never failure.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Asking for help means telling a trusted grown-up when something is too hard, too scary or going wrong — with clear words: who, what, and "help, please."

What does it mean?

Struggling in silence helps nobody: the stuck zipper stays stuck, the lost feeling stays lost, the danger stays dangerous. Asking converts a problem into a solved one in seconds — and asking EARLY, before tears, is the master move.

What does the child need to know?

Two rules in balance: TRY first (one honest attempt — the zipper pulled, the block placed), then ASK. And know your list of trusted grown-ups by name: at home, at school, in the neighborhood. Asking a NAMED person beats hoping someone notices.

Why this matters

Children who ask for help early are safer — the lost child who asks a mommy-with-children is found in minutes — and learn faster, because no struggle can hide a needed lesson. Help asked for is also never met with a sigh in families that teach this lesson.

What it teaches

Self-advocacy (the seed of every skill adults call confidence), distinguishing solvable-from-stuck, naming trusted adults, clear sentence-building, and the emotional lesson that needing others is normal, not shameful.

Words to learn

helpasktrustedgrown-uptry firstproblem

Say this to your child

“"When something is too hard or too scary, you find a grown-up you trust and say: ‘Can you help me, please?’ First you try once — then you ask. Asking is not being small; it is being smart and safe. Do you know your trusted grown-ups? Let’s say their names."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy’s palm is up, his mouth open mid-ask; the woman kneels close, listening warmly. Name both halves: the asking and the receiving.
  2. Teach the sentence in its full form: "Can you help me, please?" — plus the emergency short form: "HELP!" for real trouble.
  3. Build the trusted list together, by name: Mum, Dad, Grandma — and the school names, and the neighborhood names. A list with faces beats a rule without one.
  4. Rehearse the order: try once first, then ask — "pull the zipper once, then say help please" — so the asking rides on real effort, not instant surrender.
  5. Praise the asking itself, every time — especially when the ask came instead of a meltdown: "you ASKED — that was so smart."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy doing with his hand — fist or open palm? Is his mouth quiet or asking? What is the grown-up doing — standing far away or kneeling close? Does her face look cross or kind? Who are YOUR trusted grown-ups?

Ask your child

"What do we say when something is too hard?" "What do we try first — the zipper or the ask?" "Who are your trusted grown-ups at home? At school?" "What is the loud word for real trouble?"

What your child can say or do

"Can you help me, please?" "I tried once, then I asked!" Your child may recite the trusted list like a roll of honour, or narrate a preschool moment: "Omar asked the teacher — that was smart."

Out in the real world

Asking happens everywhere: the shop assistant who finds the right size, the librarian who reaches the high shelf, the teacher with the stuck zipper, the neighbor when a ball goes over the wall. Each real ask is a rep with a real answer.

Try it together

Help-desk game: you are the helper at a "counter"; your child brings problems — a stuck jar, a tangled toy, a hard puzzle step — with the full sentence. Swap roles so your child hears what a good ask sounds like from the receiving end.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the help sentence? What do we try first? Name two of your trusted grown-ups." The sentence, try-once, named grown-ups = landed.

Parent tips

Praise the asking, not just the solved problem — a child who is sighed at stops asking, and silent children find worse solutions. Model your own asks aloud: "I need help lifting this — watch how I ask." The list of trusted grown-ups needs refreshing each school year.

Staying safe

This lesson is a safety lesson wearing everyday clothes: teach the trusted-grown-up list as protection, the loud HELP for danger, and the rule that secrets a grown-up asks you to keep from your parents are never kept. Asking for help is also the skill behind every stranger-danger and body-safety talk to come.

This lesson pairs with the Ask for Help flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

Take Deep Breaths — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives your child the oldest calm-down tool there is, in four-year-old language: slow breaths that fill the belly, practised at calm times so the skill is waiting when big feelings arrive.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Taking deep breaths means breathing slowly IN through the nose — smelling the flower — and slowly OUT through the mouth — blowing the candle — until the body settles.

What does it mean?

Big feelings make breath fast and shallow, which tells the body MORE danger; slow deep breaths tell the body safe. Changing the breath is the fastest lever a small person can pull on a big feeling — and it needs no words at all.

What does the child need to know?

The move: one hand on the belly, in through the nose for a count of three, out through the mouth for three, three rounds. The belly should rise — that is how you know it is deep. The place to learn it is bedtime, not the meltdown.

Why this matters

A child with a rehearsed breath has somewhere to GO inside a storm. The skill only works if it exists before the storm — three rounds at bedtime build the pathway the tantrum will need. It also gives the parent a shared script: "flower and candle" works mid-crowd, mid-car, mid-crisis.

What it teaches

Self-regulation (the core executive skill), interoception (feeling breath and belly), a calm-down routine that travels, body-mind connection, and co-regulation — breathing together is attachment practice as much as technique.

Words to learn

breathedeepslowbellycalmflower

Say this to your child

“"Hands on your belly. Now smell the flower — one, two, three — and blow out the candle — one, two, three. Again, slow as honey. Feel your belly fill like a balloon? That is your calm button. We press it every night so it works when feelings get big."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy’s eyes are closed, his hands rest on his belly, his mouth makes a small o. Name the pose — this is the calm shape.
  2. Do it together: hands on bellies, smell the flower for three, blow the candle for three. Three rounds. Feel YOUR belly fill as you teach.
  3. Keep it playful at first: blow the imaginary candle, sniff the imaginary flower, swap flowers — roses, daisies, birthday candles.
  4. Make three rounds the bedtime close — the calmest moment of the day building the calmest habit.
  5. Only AFTER a week of practice, bring it to real storms: kneel, breathe audibly yourself, offer the flower — never mid-shriek on day one.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: are the boy’s eyes open or closed? Where are his hands sitting? What shape is his mouth making? Does his face look busy or quiet? Can YOUR hands find your belly the same way?

Ask your child

"What do we smell? What do we blow?" "Where does your belly go when the air comes in?" "When is our breathing practice time?" "What can we do when feelings get too big?"

What your child can say or do

"Smell the flower... blow the candle!" "My belly went up and down!" Your child may coach YOU through three rounds at lights-out, or press their own belly and whisper "calm button" mid-wobble.

Out in the real world

Calm breaths travel: the waiting room, the long car ride, the doctor’s surgery, the queue for the slide, the moment before the school gate. Flower and candle need no equipment — that is exactly why they work everywhere.

Try it together

Bubble breath: blow REAL bubbles slowly — fast breath pops nothing, slow breath makes the biggest bubble. Pinwheel and feather work the same way. The prop proves the breath, and the proof makes the practice stick.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we smell and what do we blow? Where does the air go — chest or belly? When do we practise?" Flower-candle, belly, bedtime = landed.

Parent tips

Rehearse away from the storm or the skill will not exist when needed. Breathe WITH your child audibly — your nervous system lends theirs a hand; co-regulation comes before self-regulation. If three rounds feel long, one round done is better than three refused.

Staying safe

Breathing practice is gentle — never breath-holding contests, never dizziness-as-a-game. And calm breath is a helper, not a replacement for a grown-up: if the big feeling comes from real pain or real fear, the grown-up comes first, the flower second.

This lesson pairs with the Take Deep Breaths flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Keep Your Room Safe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes your child the safety inspector of their own room: spotting trip hazards, knowing the never-touch list, and learning the rule that keeps small people safe around big problems — report, never touch.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Keeping your room safe means clearing the floor of trip hazards, keeping toys in their homes, and telling a grown-up about anything broken, spilled or dangerous — without touching it.

What does it mean?

Most room accidents are floor accidents: one block on the rug at night is a stumble waiting. And some problems are not child-sized — broken glass, spilled drinks, wall sockets — where the safe move is distance plus a loud report.

What does the child need to know?

The inspector walk: patrol the room and ask "what could someone trip on? What must never be touched?" The never-touch list: sockets, cords, heaters, broken things, spills, big people’s tools. The report line, practised until it flows: "GROWN-UP, come see!"

Why this matters

A child who reports is a child who stays safe — and who makes the whole house safer. The report-instead-of-touch rule also pre-empts the dangerous cleanup instinct: four-year-olds WANT to fix what they broke, and this lesson redirects that instinct to the person equipped.

What it teaches

Hazard perception (spotting risk before it bites), rule categorisation (touch/report), responsibility for a shared space, clear emergency sentence-building, and the good kind of pride — the helper who kept everyone on their feet.

Words to learn

safetripfloorbrokenspillreport

Say this to your child

“"Your room is yours to keep safe. Toys off the floor so nobody trips — the box is their home. And here is the big rule: if something is broken, spilled or scary-looking, you do NOT touch it. You step back and call: ‘Grown-up, come see!’ Broken things are grown-up jobs to touch and child jobs to report — and reporting is the brave job."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy is lifting a blue toy box — teddy, a red ball and blocks inside — off the floor. Name the move: toys off the floor, into the box, floor clear.
  2. Walk the room together as inspectors: your child points at trip hazards, you decide the fix together. Finding is their job; deciding is yours.
  3. Build the never-touch list out loud, room by room: sockets, cords, heaters, broken glass, spilled drinks, scissors that are not theirs.
  4. Teach and rehearse the report line with drama: "GROWN-UP, come see!" — loud, from a distance, never bringing the broken thing TO the grown-up.
  5. Practise the report on purpose: stage a "broken" crayon box tomorrow and see if the line fires. It will — and it will again when it matters.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the boy lifting — what is inside the box? Can you find the teddy? The red ball? Where will the box go? Is the floor behind him clear or messy? What do YOU see on YOUR floor tonight?

Ask your child

"What could someone trip on in your room?" "What goes on the never-touch list?" "What do we shout when something breaks?" "Why do we step back instead of picking it up?"

What your child can say or do

"Toys off the floor!" "GROWN-UP, come see — it’s broken!" Your child may inspect the hallway uninvited, report a wobbly chair leg with pride, or patrol grandma’s rug like a health-and-safety officer.

Out in the real world

Safety eyes travel: the bathroom’s wet floor, the kitchen’s spilled juice, the garden’s scattered rake, the hotel room’s mystery cords. Inspector walks work in every room of every house — and your child now owns the move.

Try it together

Safety-inspector badge: paper badge, clipboard walk of the whole house, one "hazard" you have staged per room (a shoe, a toy, a rolled sock — nothing real). Each found hazard earns the report line and a fix. The badge goes home to their door.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do with floor toys? Name two never-touch things. What is the report line?" Box-home, two right answers, the loud line = landed.

Parent tips

Thank every report warmly — a child whose report is met with a sigh learns to hide breakage, and hidden breakage is the dangerous kind. Never punish the reporting of an accident; the calm response IS the lesson. Keep the list short and real: five things remembered beat twenty listed.

Staying safe

This lesson is the safety lesson: sockets get covers, cords get chased along walls, and any real glass breakage means the child leaves the room first, barefoot never. Batteries — especially button batteries — and magnets join the never-touch list; they look like sweets and do not forgive curiosity.

This lesson pairs with the Keep Your Room Safe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Stay With a Grown-Up — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson sets the one rule that makes every outing work: stay where the grown-up can see you, hands held at the risky places — agreed before leaving home, rehearsed with kindness, with a calm plan for the rare separation.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Staying with a grown-up means keeping where your grown-up can see you, holding hands near roads and in crowds, and knowing exactly what to do if you are ever separated.

What does it mean?

Children wander because the world is interesting, not because rules failed — so the rule needs to be short enough to survive curiosity: "where I can see you." Roads and car parks are the two places hands link, because drivers cannot see small people between cars.

What does the child need to know?

The deal, agreed before every outing: eyes on, hand held at crossings and car parks, stay where the grown-up can see. And the get-found plan, rehearsed at calm times: if we ever lose each other, you stand still and shout my name — then ask a mommy-with-children or a shop worker.

Why this matters

The rule is not about mistrust — it is about visibility. A child within sight is a child a grown-up can shield. And a rehearsed plan turns the scariest "where is Mummy?" moment from panic into a procedure the child can actually run.

What it teaches

Boundary awareness (near/far, seen/unseen), rule memory under excitement, hand-holding as connection rather than capture, self-protection skills, and the trust that grows when rules are kept by BOTH sides — you stay reachable too.

Words to learn

grown-upstayhold handscrossingcar parklost

Say this to your child

“"Here is our deal: you stay where I can see you, and we hold hands near roads and in car parks — that is our agreement, before we leave the house. And if we ever, ever lose each other: you stand still and shout my name. I will come to YOU. A mommy with children or a shop worker can help you shout."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: a grown-up and a boy walk hand in hand, both smiling — she carries her bag, he carries nothing but the deal. Name the picture: this is what safe walking looks like.
  2. Agree the deal before leaving home, every time, in the same words: "eyes on, hand held, where I can see you." The ritual matters more than the words.
  3. Practise the two hand-holding zones on real walks: crossings and car parks. Same words each time until the hands reach up on their own.
  4. Rehearse the get-found plan as a game in safe places: "pretend you can’t see me — what do you do?" Stand still, shout, ask a mommy-with-children.
  5. Close the loop afterwards: "you stayed where I could see you the WHOLE trip — that is how we keep outings easy."

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: who is holding whose hand? What is the grown-up carrying? Are they walking or standing? Where are both their faces pointing — same way or different ways? Do they look worried or happy?

Ask your child

"What is our outing deal?" "Which two places always mean held hands?" "What do you do if you can’t see me?" "Who can help you shout my name?"

What your child can say or do

"Eyes on, hand held!" "I’d stand still and shout — and you’d come!" Your child may initiate the deal at the front door unprompted, or remind YOU when your eyes drift to a shop window — the rule works both ways.

Out in the real world

The rule is tested daily: the supermarket, the market crowd, the beach, the museum, the school run car park. Each outing is a rehearsal — and the rehearsed child walks taller inside the rule, because the rule makes the world explorable, not smaller.

Try it together

Find-me drill in the park: your child closes their eyes for five seconds, opens them, and points to where you are — the game trains checking-in without a single lecture. At home, stuffed animals get "lost" and the child teaches THEM the stand-still-and-shout plan.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the deal? Which two places need held hands? What do you do if we lose each other?" Eyes-on-hand-held, crossings-and-car-parks, stand-shout-ask = landed.

Parent tips

Keep the rule short enough to survive excitement — "where I can see you" beats a paragraph. Never use fear as the teacher; rehearsed plans build brave children, frightened ones freeze. Hold hands yourself at roads — the rule visibly binds both of you.

Staying safe

This lesson IS the safety lesson: car parks are the highest-risk minutes of any outing — hands link before the car door opens, every time. Teach that grown-ups HELPFUL in a separation are mommy-with-children or uniformed shop staff, and that any adult who says "keep this secret" or "don’t tell your grown-up" is automatically a tell-your-grown-up event.

This lesson pairs with the Stay With a Grown-Up flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · LIFE SKILLS & GOOD HABITS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wear Your Seat Belt — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the car-seat ritual automatic: bum in seat, belt clicked, grown-up checks — every ride, every time — and gives your child the proud half of the job and the reason behind the rule.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Wearing your seat belt means sitting in your car seat with the belt across your chest and lap, clicked shut — checked by a grown-up before the car moves, every single ride.

What does it mean?

Cars stop suddenly sometimes — that is what brakes are for — and an unbuckled body keeps moving when the car stops. The car seat holds the body the way arms hold a sleeping baby: snug is safe. The click is not a suggestion; it is the machine’s only promise.

What does the child need to know?

The ritual in order: bum in seat, belt over chest and lap, CLICK, grown-up check, then "safe to go!" Two jobs: your child does the climb and the click; the grown-up does the final check — both jobs matter, and neither replaces the other.

Why this matters

The rule is absolute because rides are unpredictable and habits are not: no click, no ride — even for the shortest trip, even when protesting, even for one street. A rule with no exceptions needs no renegotiation at the doorstep, which is exactly what makes it easy.

What it teaches

Routine mastery with a real safety stake, body awareness (belt across chest bone and lap bones, never the tummy), cause-and-effect thinking, patience at the doorstep, and the identity of being someone who is "safe to go."

Words to learn

seat beltcar seatclickbucklechecksafe to go

Say this to your child

“"Bum in seat, belt across your chest, click — and then I check, because checking is my half of the job. When every belt in the car is clicked, the car is allowed to go. No click, no ride — not because you are in trouble, but because that is the car’s one rule for everybody."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: the boy sits in his dark car seat, the belt crossing his chest, the red buckle clicked at his lap, hands resting calm. Name every part — this is the finished picture.
  2. Walk the ritual at the real car: bum in seat, belt over, click. Your child does the click; you do the check and say "safe to go!"
  3. Teach the belt’s geography: across the chest BONE and the lap BONES — never across the tummy or behind the back.
  4. Make the click the finish line of boarding: nobody starts the engine, nobody tells a story, until the check is done. The routine teaches itself through repetition.
  5. Answer every protest with the same calm sentence: "the car only moves when every belt is clicked" — the predictability is the comfort.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: where is the boy sitting — a big seat or a special one? What crosses his chest? What color is the buckle button? Where are his hands? Does he look squished or comfy? Whose job was the click — his or the grown-up’s?

Ask your child

"What are the two jobs before the car moves?" "Where does the belt sit — tummy or bones?" "What do we say after the click?" "Does the rule take holidays for short trips?"

What your child can say or do

"Click — safe to go!" "Did you check MY belt? Check it!" Your child may refuse to let the engine start until the check is said out loud, or click a teddy into a toy car with the whole ritual, check included.

Out in the real world

The ritual travels: the family car, grandma’s car, the taxi (booster carried along), the school-run carpool. Same click, same check — the rule rides in every vehicle, and your child becomes its loudest enforcer.

Try it together

Car-seat drill: a toy car, a teddy, a ribbon belt. Your child runs the full ritual — seat, belt, click, grown-up check — then swaps and plays the checker on YOU. The checker role builds the inspector who will one day out-click you.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the ritual steps? Whose job is the final check? Does the rule bend for short trips?" Bum-belt-click, grown-up, never = landed.

Parent tips

Build the ritual into the routine so there is nothing to argue about — the click is how boarding ENDS, not a favour. Praise the self-click, keep the check sacred, and never start the car mid-protest: moving vehicles and moving goalposts both teach the wrong lesson.

Staying safe

Children ride in car seats or boosters until the adult belt fits properly — which is later than it looks; the grown-up check happens every single ride. Bulky winter coats flatten under belts — buckle first, blanket over. And the car never moves until every belt in it is clicked: groceries ride in the boot, not on laps.

This lesson pairs with the Wear Your Seat Belt flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Life Skills & Good Habits (Class 32).
